title: The Built Environment and Spatial Form
authors: Denise L. Lawrence and Setha M. Low, 1990
review_question: To define the major areas of research in the field of the built environment and spatial form in terms of issues and theoretical approach, critically evaluating major contributions, and suggesting directions for future research.
inclusion_exclusion_criteria: The review focuses on the built environment and spatial form, including built forms (building types, defined/bounded spaces, landmarks, specific building elements, spatial subdivisions) and site plans. It explicitly excludes human relations with the natural environment and landscape, large-scale settlement patterns, material culture (moveable nature), traditional arts, and applied anthropology addressing housing issues in developing countries.

findings.antecedent: Built forms (dwelling plan, size, number, types of rooms, shape, permanence)
findings.consequent: Social organization (size and composition of resident group, postmarital residence, social complexity, specialization, stratification, activity areas, economic and social cooperation, gender relations)
findings.quote: a significant body of literature has examined a consistent set of questions regarding the interactions of the built environment with social organization and spatial behavior.

findings.antecedent: Built environment (forms, site plans, physical attributes, spatial organization, architectural elements)
findings.consequent: Expression of culturally shared mental structures and processes, meaning, social or political status, social structure, cosmology, group identity, individual identity, values, social relations, aesthetic theories
findings.quote: Symbolic approaches interpret the built environment as an expression of culturally shared mental structures and processes.

findings.antecedent: Built environment, spatial dimensions, spatial configurations, physical features
findings.consequent: Concepts of the self, nonverbal behavior, cognition and language, spatial perception and orientation, mental health, privacy, territoriality, personal identity, human development
findings.quote: A somewhat loose collection of what might be called "psychological" interpretations of human interactions with the built environment have focused on concepts of the self, spatial dimensions of nonverbal behavior, and cognition and language.

findings.antecedent: Social, political, and economic forces, history and evolution, social institutions, power, capital accumulation, urban planning, colonial planning
findings.consequent: Built environment (forms, urban phenomena, settlement patterns), social action, social reproduction, class, gender, race, and culture relations
findings.source: SOCIAL PRODUCTION OF BUILT FORM section
findings.quote: Theories of the social production of built form focus on the social, political, and economic forces that produce the built environment, and conversely, the impact of the socially produced built environment on social action.

synthesis_conclusions: Social and cultural studies of human interactions with the built environment have grown significantly and are likely to receive more attention.
The area of social production theories is identified as the most promising new direction for anthropologists.

The reintegration of spatial and temporal dimensions into social theory (by Bourdieu, Foucault, Giddens) provides a means to integrate the analysis of the built environment, its role, and its meaning in society.
Buildings, especially dwellings, serve human needs and are focal points for personal and social identities.
The analysis of building decisions and symbolic meaning must be understood in conjunction with social, economic, and institutional forces, as well as history.
Anthropologists should examine architectural researchers' detailed documentation and descriptive techniques for built forms.
Theories of metaphor and designed architectural forms offer a fruitful starting point for collaboration between anthropologists and design professionals, focusing on aesthetics, form, and production.
evidence_gaps: Theoretical development and empirical work across research areas are uneven.
Concrete data are often missing, particularly for social production theories.
The meaning of the built environment, as revealed through metaphorical connections and ritual practices, is an important but incompletely explored dimension.
The processes by which decisions are made to build, remodel, or move are neither well documented nor understood in most societies studied by anthropologists.
Psychological treatments of human interactions with the built environment have received mild anthropological interest.
Early anthropological inquiries into perception and language have not been pursued by later researchers, nor has the development of proxemic research been fully explored.
limitations: Theoretical development and empirical work across the reviewed areas are uneven.
Concrete data are often missing, especially in social production theories.
The meaning of the built environment through metaphor and ritual is incompletely explored.
Decision-making processes for building, remodeling, or moving are poorly documented in many societies.
No single theoretical approach is perfectly adequate on its own.
Anthropological interest in psychological treatments of the built environment has been mild.
Early research on spatial perception, language, and proxemics has not been fully explored by later anthropologists.

theory_commitments.theory_name: Cultural Ecology of the Built Environment
theory_commitments.specific_claim: The built environment is a culturally organized system that mediates human-environment interactions and shapes social life.

mechanism_chain.description: Built forms influence social organization through culturally mediated meanings and the affordances they provide for human behavior.
